extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys and agents), USPTO disciplinary counsel, and practitioners subject to USPTO professional conduct rules
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules the USPTO (OED) and Administrative Law Judge apply to evaluate practitioner misconduct and to determine sanctions (including service/answer requirements, specific regulatory violations under 37 C.F.R., and the factors considered in imposing sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file an answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in an entry of default judgment." 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If notice is served by publication, an answer is due within 30 days from the completion of the second publication; failing to answer leads to being deemed to have admitted the Complaint's allegations and may produce default judgment. The decision cites the respondent's failure to file an answer and consequent default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by publication when mail/email unsuccessful (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the OED Director is unable to serve by mail, service may be made via publication pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in this case: Notices were published in the Official Gazette for two consecutive weeks (Dec 27, 2016 and Jan 3, 2017); publication starts the timeline for an answer. The decision documents attempts to serve by certified mail and email before resorting to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide and keep current mailing/email address (37 C.F.R. § 11.11 implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide the Office with address information as required by 37 C.F.R. § 11.11; service was attempted at addresses and email the respondent had previously provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mail to the provided address is returned (e.g., 'Return to Sender', 'Unclaimed', 'Unable to Forward') or email is undelivered, the Office may use alternative service methods (including publication); failing to maintain accurate contact info can lead to successful service and adverse default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to respond to OED Request for Information / cooperate with investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.22 and § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: OED mailed a Request for Information and Evidence under 37 C.F.R. § 11.22; failure to respond to a lawful request for information from OED violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The First RFI requested information within a 30-day deadline; subsequent Notices extended time but respondent still failed to respond. The Court treated failure to respond as misconduct and an aggravating factor (bad faith obstruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform client of Office correspondence (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8): It is misconduct to fail to inform a client of correspondence received from the Office when the correspondence (i) could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office; (ii) is received by the practitioner on behalf of a client or former client; and (iii) is correspondence of which a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances the client should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office Actions and Notices of Abandonment are treated as correspondence a reasonable practitioner would notify the client about. In this case respondent received Office Actions and Notices of Abandonment and did not inform clients, constituting violation of § 10.23(a)/(b)/(c)(8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 10.77)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77 proscribes neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision finds neglect where respondent received Office Actions but took no action, allowed applications to become abandoned without notifying clients, and thereby violated § 10.77(c). Neglect can include failing to respond to rejections and restriction requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to act with reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 proscribes failing to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific example: failing to file the nonprovisional and PCT application within one year of the provisional (thus missing priority) was held to violate § 11.103. Diligence includes timely prosecution and meeting statutory/time-limited deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failing to keep client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) proscribes failing to keep the client reasonably informed about the status of a matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent did not inform clients of Office Actions, Notices of Abandonment, or the filing/granting of Petitions to Revive; such failures violate § 11.104(a)(3). Keeping clients reasonably informed includes advising of adverse developments and revival filings/grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of third-party funds — prompt notice and delivery (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d) requires that upon receiving funds in which a third party has an interest, a practitioner must promptly notify and deliver to the third party any funds that the third party is entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent received approximately $100,000 to be forwarded to foreign associates (J.A. Kemp, CPA Global) for annuity payments but did not forward funds ($82,508.14 remained unpaid), violating § 11.115(d). Guidance: practitioners must hold and promptly transmit third-party funds for their intended purpose and provide notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements to a tribunal / failure to correct (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) proscribes making false statements of fact or law to a tribunal or failing to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here, respondent claimed an incorrect priority date in related applications and put incorrect dates into application specifications; such misstatements to the Office violate § 11.303(a)(1). Practitioners must not make or leave uncorrected material misrepresentations to the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements to others in connection with representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.401(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.401(a) proscribes making false statements to another in connection with the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent provided Ms. Logue incorrect information about the filing date of the provisional application; that misrepresentation violates § 11.401(a). This extends beyond tribunals to communications with third parties and co-counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging in dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats the pattern of misrepresenting filing dates and allowing applications to be abandoned without client knowledge as conduct involving dishonesty and deceit, warranting disciplinary measures under § 11.804(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when imposing sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (I) whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court applied these four factors: found duty violations to clients/patent bar; respondent acted intentionally/knowingly; actual injuries included lost rights and monetary loss ($82,508.14 annuity payments); and numerous aggravating factors existed. The Court also looks to the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions (2005) when assessing aggravating/mitigating circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (examples used in sanction analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of aggravating factors considered: bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding (intentional failure to respond to RFI and Court order), failure to appear, dishonest or selfish motive, indifference to making restitution, commission of multiple offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats these as magnifying circumstances supporting a severe sanction (exclusion). The presence of intentional concealment, withholding client funds, and refusal to cooperate are emphasized as especially severe aggravators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible sanctions and reinstatement conditions (exclusion and restitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanction outcome in this case: exclusion from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters. Reinstatement may be conditioned upon restitution to clients, among other conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court concluded that exclusion (disbarment from practice before USPTO) was warranted given the violations and aggravating factors. Reinstatement is possible but may require restitution and other conditions per the Court's discretion.
